title: Listening Post Bravo
subtitle: What the Armor Leaves Behind · Chapter 26 of 40
content:
Danse had already recorded a goodbye.

I found the holotape beside his tags.

He reached for it when he realized what I was looking at.

I got there first.

“Give me that.”

“No.”

His face hardened.

“That is personal.”

“So is asking me to shoot you.”

“You don’t have the right—”

“I have every right if you were planning to leave me this instead of a conversation.”

He stopped.

The holotape felt impossibly small in my hand.

I did not play it.

I did not need to.

Danse looked away.

“I needed to put things in order.”

“You arranged your own execution.”

“Maxson arranged it.”

“You agree with him.”

“Yes.”

The answer came without hesitation.

It broke my heart.

“Why?”

“You know why.”

“I want to hear you say it.”

His eyes snapped back to mine.

“Because synths are dangerous. Because the Institute builds machines that replace people. Because technology without limits destroyed the world once and the Institute is determined to do it again.”

“And you?”

“I am one of those machines.”

“You’ve spent years fighting them.”

“That could be programming.”

“You loved Cutler.”

“Implanted memory.”

“You care about Haylen.”

“Programming.”

“You get angry at Rhys.”

Despite everything, his mouth twitched.

I stepped closer.

“You make disgusting coffee.”

“That proves nothing.”

“You hate canned crab.”

“Everyone should.”

“You flirt like a malfunctioning protectron.”

His eyes widened.

I kept going before he could stop me.

“You laugh when you forget not to. You count casualties until they become weights tied around your ribs. You write maintenance notes in block letters. You pretend every kind thing you do is logistics. You’re terrified of losing people, and somehow your solution is to volunteer to become one more person we lose.”

Danse’s face broke.

“You don’t know if any of that is real.”

“I don’t know if any of my memories mean what I think they mean either.”

“That is not the same.”

“No. But real is not the same as original.”

He stared at me.

I moved close enough that only a step remained between us.

“If someone gave you memories, you still made choices with them.”

“My choices were based on a lie.”

“Welcome to being alive.”

Anger flashed.

“Don’t trivialize this.”

“I’m not.”

“Everything I am could have been manufactured.”

“And everything you’ve done since wasn’t.”

“You can’t know that.”

“Neither can you.”

Silence.

There it was again.

Uncertainty.

The thing he hated most.

Danse sat heavily on the cot.

“I don’t have parents.”

The sentence came out so quietly I nearly missed it.

I sat beside him.

“I thought I just didn’t remember them. I told myself the Wasteland does that. People disappear. Families break apart.”

His hands clenched.

“But there may never have been anyone. Those sons of bitches couldn’t even give me that.”

I wanted to tell him memories did not make family.

That sounded too clean.

So I said, “That hurts.”

He looked at me.

“Yes.”

“I’m sorry.”

His shoulders shook once.

Danse covered his face with both hands.

I sat beside him and did nothing heroic.

No speech.

No solution.

Eventually he leaned into me.

I wrapped my arms around him.

He held on hard enough to hurt.

I did not complain.

Minutes passed.

When he finally pulled back, his eyes were wet.

He looked ashamed.

I hated that more than anything.

“Don’t,” I said.

“What?”

“Apologize.”

“I wasn’t going to.”

“You were thinking it.”

“I notice patterns.”

A tiny, broken smile.

There he was.

I took his hand.

“Come with me.”

“Where?”

“Out.”

“I can’t go back.”

“Then not back.”

“Maxson will come.”

“Let him.”

Danse’s expression hardened.

“I won’t have you branded a traitor because of me.”

“Too late. I’m emotionally compromised.”

“This isn’t a joke.”

“No.”

I looked directly at him.

“I am not killing you.”

He looked at our joined hands.

“What happens if I’m wrong?” he asked.

“About what?”

“What if there’s something inside me the Institute can activate? A command. A switch.”

Fear crawled cold along my back.

Possible did not mean likely.

But Danse needed truth, not comfort.

“Then we deal with it if it happens.”

“That’s not enough.”

“It has to be.”

He closed his eyes.

For once, there was no plan.

No certainty.

Just the next choice.

When he opened them again, he whispered, “I don’t want to die.”

My throat closed.

“Good.”

The word shook.

Danse gripped my hand.

“I don’t know what to do.”

“We start by leaving the bunker.”

He looked toward the door.

Then back at me.

Slowly, he stood.

That was when the elevator above us began to move.

Danse went pale.

“Maxson.”

I reached for my weapon.

Danse caught my wrist.

“No.”

Footsteps approached down the corridor.

The bunker door opened.

Elder Maxson stepped inside.

The elevator had not yet reached the lower level.

We had maybe thirty seconds.

Danse used them to become a paladin again.

He picked up his rifle, checked the charge, straightened the collar of the uniform Maxson had already taken from him in every way that mattered.

“Put the weapon down,” I said.

“I’m not going to fire.”

“Then why hold it?”

His eyes met mine.

Because his hands needed something familiar.

I understood.

“Fine. Keep the rifle pointed at the floor.”

“That was already my intention.”

“Humor me.”

He shifted the barrel down.

The elevator machinery groaned closer.

Danse looked toward the corridor.

“You should tell him I deceived you.”

“No.”

“It may protect your standing.”

“No.”

“Listen to me.”

“I am.”

“If Maxson believes you knowingly aided a synth—”

“I knowingly aided *you*.”

His face tightened.

“That distinction will not matter to him.”

“It matters to me.”

“You are being irrational.”

“So are you.”

“I am accepting the consequences of what I am.”

“No. You are using your favorite moral shortcut.”

Anger flashed through the despair.

“What does that mean?”

“It means you would rather punish yourself than live with uncertainty.”

Danse stared at me.

The elevator stopped.

A warning light turned green.

We had seconds now.

I stepped close enough to catch the front of his uniform in my fist.

“You don’t get to decide that dying is honorable just because living is complicated.”

His mouth opened.

The doors above slid apart.

Footsteps.

Danse whispered, “You don’t understand what you’re asking.”

“I’m asking you to survive long enough to find out.”

Then Maxson entered.

The confrontation lasted minutes.

It also seemed to contain every argument Danse and I had ever had.

Categories.

Orders.

Personhood.

Whether loyalty mattered more than origin.

Whether a life could be real if its beginning was manufactured.

When Maxson said the Institute could activate Danse at any time, I saw the fear strike him again.

Not fear of being killed.

Fear of hurting us.

Danse lowered his rifle to the floor.

“Then keep me confined,” he said. “Study me. If I exhibit any sign of hostile programming—”

Maxson’s expression turned to stone.

“We do not study abominations in the hope they become acceptable.”

I felt Danse flinch beside me.

The word mattered because he had used it himself.

About others.

About beings he had never known.

Now it was his.

I looked at him.

He understood that too.

For the first time, I saw the full collision between his old beliefs and his own heartbeat.

It did not make him enlightened.

It made him devastated.

Maxson ordered me to step aside.

I did not.

Danse ordered me to obey.

I did not.

The absurdity might have been funny anywhere else.

When Maxson’s hand finally left his weapon and the sentence changed from execution to exile, Danse looked almost disappointed.

That terrified me.

He had prepared himself for death so completely that survival felt like a failure of procedure.

After Maxson left and Danse collapsed against me, I held him until feeling returned to his hands.

He stared at the open bunker door.

“I should go after him.”

“No.”

“I need to explain—”

“He knows.”

“Then apologize.”

“For existing?”

Danse closed his eyes.

The answer was yes.

I put my hand against his chest.

His heartbeat was fast beneath the uniform.

“Feel that.”

He frowned.

“What?”

“Your heart.”

“That proves biological function, not—”

“I am not making a philosophical point.”

He stopped.

“I am telling you that right now, in this room, you are alive.”

His breath caught.

“Whatever you decide about everything else can wait until tomorrow.”

“I don’t know if I can.”

“Then decide in ten-minute increments.”

Danse looked at me.

“Ten minutes?”

“Can you not kill yourself for ten minutes?”

Pain moved across his face.

“Yes.”

“Good. After that, we negotiate another ten.”

“That’s ridiculous.”

“Probably.”

He let out a breath that almost became a laugh.

I kept my palm over his heart.

Ten minutes passed.

Then another.

By the time the bunker lights cycled to night mode, Danse had survived the first evening of the rest of his life.

Not because he believed he deserved it.

Because, for twenty minutes at a time, he trusted me enough to postpone the verdict.
